title: Serving stack operator effort matrix and messaging brief
content:
Goal: Provide a compact operator-focused comparison of common self-hosted inference stacks (vLLM/TGI/TensorRT-LLM style), translate operator effort into GTM messaging, and give concrete pushback / trial designs for build-vs-buy conversations.

Executive summary (for AE / SE):
- High-level claim to use: "Self-hosted stacks can save marginal compute dollars but transfer large, recurring operator and product risk to your team. Redwood minimizes that operational delta with a predictable, observable, and SLAs-backed inference runtime."
- Thesis: Buyers who are primarily cost-driven and have <2 FTEs for inference ops are poor candidates for long-term self-hosting. Buyers who are regulation-driven (air-gapped, KMS/HSM needs) but have >3 FTEs and strong infra maturity may want private deployments — offer Redwood Private as a compromise.

Operator effort matrix (qualitative):
- Columns: initial-setup, ongoing-tuning, kernel/debug, model-upgrades, security-hardening, monitoring/alerting, capacity-planning, incident-response
- vLLM (open-source serving + homegrown wrappers):
  - initial-setup: High (compile from source, CUDA/cuDNN/transformer kernel compatibility)
  - ongoing-tuning: High (memory management, batch policy tuning)
  - kernel/debug: Very High (GPU OOMs, custom kernel patches, sequence-length regressions)
  - model-upgrades: Medium-High (weights + tokenizer changes break caching)
  - security-hardening: Medium (need to bolt on KMS and audit chains)
  - monitoring/alerting: Low-Medium (basic Prometheus; lacks token-level cost plumbing)
  - capacity-planning: High (manual profiling, headroom overcommit)
  - incident-response: High (cold start, KV cache invalidation pain)
- TGI (NVIDIA Text Generation Inference):
  - initial-setup: Medium (official binaries, but GPU and driver compatibility needed)
  - ongoing-tuning: Medium (quantization/precision tuning needed for performance)
  - kernel/debug: Medium-High (vendor drivers, TensorRT behaviors)
  - model-upgrades: Medium (supported formats, conversion steps)
  - security-hardening: Medium-High (enterprise options available but integration work)
  - monitoring/alerting: Medium (basic telemetry, limited token-level traces)
  - capacity-planning: Medium (good throughput, but tuning for mixed workloads is manual)
  - incident-response: Medium (vendor logs help but ops still needed)
- TensorRT-LLM (highly-optimized vendor kernels):
  - initial-setup: Very High (specialized conversion, TensorRT engines, driver/kernel matching)
  - ongoing-tuning: High (engine rebuilds per model/sequence profile)
  - kernel/debug: Very High (low-level CUDA/TensorRT debugging)
  - model-upgrades: High (reconversions required for every major weight change)
  - security-hardening: Medium (depends on infra; HSM integration non-trivial)
  - monitoring/alerting: Low-Medium (needs custom hooks)
  - capacity-planning: High (different engines for different prompt distributions)
  - incident-response: Very High (failover is brittle without fallback stacks)

Quantitative signals to surface in sales conversations (benchmarks to demand from prospects):
- p50/p95/p99 token latency at representative sequence lengths (16/128/512) and concurrency (1, 8, 32).
- tokens/sec per GPU under steady-state and under bursty arrival patterns.
- cold-start time for new model pods and impact of KV cache warm-up on latency.
- operator FTE per 10 production models to maintain 99% availability. Suggested conservative baseline: 0.5-1.0 FTE/model-year for mature infra; 1.5-3.0 FTE/model-year for open-source stacks (vLLM-like) at scale.
- mean time to recovery (MTTR) for kernel/driver-induced outages.

Key engineer-facing friction stories (short, punchy):
1) You save 10% on per-token compute but spend months tuning batch windows and patching CUDA bugs — total TCO beats just compute savings in 6–9 months.
2) Models change fast (adapter weights, tokenizer fixes) — every model tweak can break optimized engines and invalidate caching assumptions.
3) Multi-tenant or multi-model fleets amplify tail latency — naive autoscale leads to wasted GPUs or degraded SLOs.

Positioning hooks per persona: 
- Startup ML Engineer (single-team): "Deploy quickly, validate model choice, and iterate without investing ops cycles on infra. Redwood hosted lets your team focus on product experiments and get meaningful latency/cost visibility out of the box."
- Platform/Infra Team: "Standardize runtimes across teams, enforce routing/fallback policies, and eliminate ad-hoc kernel patching. Redwood Dedicated gives predictable throughput and autoscaling guardrails."
- Security/Compliance/Legal: "Private deployments with KMS/HSM integrations, audit logs, and network controls so you don't trade compliance for performance."

Battlecard rebuttals to common self-hosted objections: 
- "We already have GPUs and want to use them." -> Rebuttal: Great — most customers start there. But surface the ongoing incremental costs: ops FTE, driver/OS maintenance, emergency on-call, and rework for each model conversion. Offer a pilot where we run the same workload against Redwood Dedicated and report end-to-end cost and MTTR.
- "We’ll save money in the long run." -> Rebuttal: Ask for a 12–18 month total-cost forecast that includes personnel overhead and reliability risk. Propose a modeled example: 3 engineers @ $180k fully burdened supporting a fleet -> $540k/year overhead; compare to Redwood reserved capacity pricing.
- "We need on-prem for data residency." -> Rebuttal: Redwood Private and on-prem packages are designed for this — highlight differences (we manage the control plane and observability, you keep data plane).

Suggested 2-week technical trial (SE playbook):
1) Agree on 3 representative prompts (short chat, medium doc, long seq) and traffic shape.
2) Run baseline on their target self-hosted stack (vLLM/TGI/TensorRT) with simple telemetry that captures p95/p99.
3) Run same workload on Redwood hosted/dedicated/private with identical model artifacts (weights + tokenizer).
4) Produce an apples-to-apples report: tokens/sec, cost/GPU-hour, p99 latency, tail latency under burst, and an ops-effort estimate (time spent on tuning/conversions/bug fixes).
5) Leave a checklist for the prospect: operator tasks avoided by using Redwood (kernel patching, engine rebuilds, KV cache tuning, multi-model routing, SLA runbook).

Suggested GTM messaging snippets (short):
- "Ship LLM features, not GPU debugging."
- "Predictable inference economics — not just lower compute bills."
- "Turn model upgrades into a release, not an incident."

Edge-case failure modes (use in technical objections):
- Model conversion regressions: optimized engine produces different logits due to precision/quantization differences — requires QA and rollbacks.
- KV cache invalidation: partial warm caches across autoscaled replicas lead to inconsistent latency spikes.
- Driver/OS upgrades: vendor driver upgrades cause runtime downtimes; often only visible at scale and require kernel-level bisects.

Competitive differentiators to emphasize vs self-hosted demos:
- End-to-end token-level cost and latency visibility (not just GPU utilization).
- Automatic, workload-aware batching and prefix/KV caching tuned by runtime telemetry.
- Routing policies and automatic fallback to compatible variants when capacity constrained.
- Managed upgrades and validated model conversion paths to reduce MTTR.
- SLA-backed Dedicated tiers and Private deployment options for regulated customers.

Open questions / next steps for product/SE partnership:
- Build a short benchmark harness SEs can drop into prospect environments to capture the baseline metrics (scripted p95/p99 runs, concurrency generators).
- Create a 1-pager ops-effort calculator (inputs: number of models, expected QPS, average sequence length, desired p99) that outputs estimated FTE/year for self-hosted stacks.
- Collate customer stories where the self-hosted cost-savings claim turned into unexpected ops costs.

Appendix: quick checklist of operator tasks (for use in discovery):
- Driver / CUDA / cuDNN upgrades and compatibility testing
- Model conversion and correctness testing (float32 -> quantized / TRT engine)
- KV cache warm-up and cache invalidation policies
- Batching policy tuning for mixed-length traffic
- Autoscaler rules and cold-start mitigation
- Token-level cost accounting and billing plumbing
- Rollout and fallback policies for model versions
- Incident runbooks for GPU OOM / kernel panic

Notes to SEs: copy/paste the friction stories and the 2-week trial plan into demo proposals. Keep the operator matrix handy and use the benchmark ask as a hard requirement in any cost-savings discussion.

Document owner: Alyssa Chen (go-to-market). This is a working draft — feedback welcome from SEs and product on the ops-effort baseline numbers.
